<li class="note" id="note-10" role="doc-endnote"><p>The reader may guess the meaning.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-10" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-11" role="doc-endnote"><p>A gold ring was worn by the Equites; and accordingly to desire the gold ring is the same as to desire to be raised to the Equestrian class.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-11" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-12" role="doc-endnote"><p>The colophon. See ii. 14. note 5. After the words <q>most splendid slavery</q> it is probable that some words have accidentally been omitted in the MSS.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-12" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-13" role="doc-endnote"><p>Compare i 2. 6.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-13" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-14" role="doc-endnote"><p>Compare i. 22</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-14" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-15" role="doc-endnote"><p>Sic praetextatos referunt Artaxata mores.—Juv. ii. 170. See Epict. i. 2, note 4.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-15" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-16" role="doc-endnote"><p>Saturnalia. See i. 25, note 3.</p> 
<p>At this season the slaves had liberty to enjoy themselves and to talk freely with their masters. Hence Horace says, <span class="cit"> <cite>Sat. ii. 74—</cite> <span class="verse-quote" lang="lat" class="foreign"><span class="lg"> <span class="l">Age. libertate Decembri,</span> <span class="l">Quando ita majores voluerunt, utere.</span> </span></span> </span></p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-16" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-17" role="doc-endnote"><p><q lang="lat" class="foreign">Insigne hoc exemplum est <span class="foreign" lang="grc">τοῦ εἰκῆ τὰς προλήψεις ἐφαρμόζειν ταῖς ἐπι μέρους οὐσίαις</span>. De quo, vide i. 22, 9, ii. 11, 3, ii. 17, 7.</q> Upton.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-17" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-18" role="doc-endnote"><p>Schweighaeuser observes that death is in our power, as the Stoics taught; and Epictetus often tells us that the door is open. He suggests that the true reading may be <span class="foreign" lang="grc">καὶ οὐκ ἀποθανεῖν</span>. I think that the text is right. Epictetus asks is <q>Life or death</q> in our power. He means no more than if he had said Life only.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-18" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-19" role="doc-endnote"><p>He means that which seems to you to be false. See iii. 22, 42.</p> 
<p><q>In the matter of assent then</q>: this is the third <span class="foreign" lang="grc">τόρος</span> or <q>locus</q> or division in philosophy (iii. 2, 1–5). As to the Will, compare i. 17, note 10. Epictetus affirms that a man cannot be compelled to assent, that is to admit, to allow, or, to use another word, to believe in that which seems to him to be false, or, to use the same word again, to believe in that in which he does not believe. When the Christian uses the two creeds, which begin with the words, <q>I believe etc.,</q> he knows or he ought to know, that he cannot compel an unbeliever to accept the same belief. He may by pains and penalties of various kinds compel some persons to profess or to express the same belief: but as no pains or penalties could compel some Christians to deny their belief, so I suppose that perhaps there are men who could not be compelled to express this belief when they have it not. The case of the believer and the unbeliever however are not the same. The believer may be strengthened in his belief by the belief that he will in some way be punished by God, if he denies that which he believes. The unbeliever will not have the same motive or reason for not expressing his assent to that which he does not believe. He believes that it is and will be all the same to him with respect to God, whether he gives his assent to that which he does not believe or refuses his assent. There remains nothing then to trouble him if he expresses his assent to that which he does not believe, except the opinion of those who know that he does not believe, or his own reflections on expressing his assent to that which he does not believe; or in other words his publication of a lie, which may probably do no harm to any man or in any way. I believe that some men are strong enough, under some circumstances at least, to refuse their assent to any thing which they do not believe; but I do not affirm that they would do this under all circumstances.</p> 
<p>To return to the matter under consideration, a man cannot be compelled by any power to accept voluntarily a thing as true, when lie believes that it is not true; and this act of his is quite independent of the matter whether his unbelief is well founded or not. He does not believe because he cannot believe. Yet it is said (Mark xvi. 11,) in the received text, as it now stands, <q>He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not, shall be damned</q> (condemned). The cause, as it is called, of this unbelief is explained by some theologians; but all men do not admit the explanation to be sufficient: and it does not concern the present subject.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-19" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-20" role="doc-endnote"><p>The word <q>admire</q> is <span class="foreign" lang="grc">θαυμάσῃς</span> in the original. The word is often used by Epictetus, and Horace uses <q>admirari</q> in this Stoical sense. See i. 29. 2, note.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-20" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-21" role="doc-endnote"><p>See Schweig.’s note on <span class="foreign" lang="grc">μέρος</span>.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-21" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-22" role="doc-endnote"><p>The word is <span class="foreign" lang="grc">ἀγγαρεία</span>, a word of Persian origin (Herodotus, viii. 98). It means here the seizure of animals for military purposes when it is necessary. Upton refers to Matthew 5, v 41, Mark 15, c. 21 for similar uses of the verb <span class="foreign" lang="grc">ἀγγαρεύω</span></p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-22" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-23" role="doc-endnote"><p>Here he speaks of asses being shod. The Latin translation of the word (<span class="foreign" lang="grc">ὑποδημάτια</span>) in Epictetus is <q>ferreas calces</q>. I suppose they could use nothing but iron.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-23" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-24" role="doc-endnote"><p>See Schweig.’s note.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-24" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-25" role="doc-endnote"><p>See Schweig.’s note.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-25" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-26" role="doc-endnote"><p>Schweig. suggests <span class="foreign" lang="grc">καταβεβλήκαμεν</span> instead of <span class="foreign" lang="grc">ἀποβεβλήκαμεν</span>, though all his MSS. have the word in the text. I do not think that his proposed alteration is an improvement.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-26" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-27" role="doc-endnote"><p>The word is <span class="foreign" lang="grc">ἀποτειχίζω</span>, which means what I have translated. The purpose of circumvallation was to take and sometimes also to destroy a fortress. Schweig. translates the word by <q>destruam,</q> and that is perhaps not contrary to the meaning of the text; but it is not the exact meaning of the word.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-27" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-28" role="doc-endnote"><p>In this passage and in what follows we find the emphatic affirmation of the duty of conformity and of the subjection of man’s will to the will of God. The words are conclusive evidence of the doctrine of Epictetus that a man ought to subject himself in all things to the will of God or to that which he believes to be the will of God. No Christian martyr ever proclaimed a more solemn obedience to God’s will. The Christian martyr indeed has given perfect proof of his sincerity by enduring torments and death: the heathen philosopher was not put to the same test, and we cannot therefore say that he would have been able to bear it.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-28" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-29" role="doc-endnote"><p>In this passage the distinction must be observed between <span class="foreign" lang="grc">θέλω</span> and <span class="foreign" lang="grc">βουλομαι</span>, which the Latin translators have not observed, nor Mrs. Carter. See Schweig.’s note on s. 90.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-29" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-30" role="doc-endnote"><p><span class="foreign" lang="grc">ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ</span>: he means <q>on earth.</q></p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-30" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-31" role="doc-endnote"><p>Schweig. expresses his surprise that Epictetus has applied this word (<span class="foreign" lang="grc">ὁρμάς</span>) to God. He says that Wolf has translated it <q lang="lat" class="foreign">Dei appetitionem,</q> and Upton <q lang="lat" class="foreign">impetum.</q> He says that he has translated it <q lang="lat" class="foreign">consilium.</q></p> 
<p>It is not unusual for men to speak of God in the same words in which they speak of man.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-31" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-32" role="doc-endnote"><p>See ii. 1. 18. Schweig. expected that Epictetus would have said <q>body and possessions etc.</q> I assume that Epictetus did say <q>body and possessions etc.,</q> and that his pupil or some copyist of MSS. has omitted the word <q>body.</q></p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-32" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-33" role="doc-endnote"><p><q>The Lord gave and the Lord hath taken away. Job i. 21.</q> Mrs. Carter.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-33" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-34" role="doc-endnote"><p>The initiated (<span class="foreign" lang="grc">μύσται</span>) are those who were introduced with solemn ceremonies into some great religious body. These ceremonies are described by Dion Prus. Orat. xii., quoted by Upton.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-34" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-35" role="doc-endnote"><p><q>And is this all the comfort, every serious reader will be apt to say, which one of the best philosophers, in one of his noblest discourses, can give to the good man under severe distress? <q>Either tell yourself that present suffering void of future hope, is no evil, or give up your existence and mingle with the elements of the Universe</q>! Unspeakably more rational and more worthy of infinite goodness is our blessed Master’s exhortation to the persecuted Christian: <q>Rejoice and be exceedingly glad, for great is your reward in heaven.</q></q> Mrs. Carter.</p> 
<p>I do not think that Mrs. Carter has represented correctly the teaching of Epictetus. He is addressing men who were not Christians, but were, as he assumes, believers in God or in the Gods, and his argument is that a man ought to be contented with things as they are, because they are from God. If he cannot be contented with things as they are, and make the best of them, the philosopher can say no more to the man. He tells him to depart. What else could he say to a grumbler, who is also a believer in God? If he is not a believer, Epictetus might say the same to him also. The case is past help or advice.</p> 
<p>The Christian doctrine, of which probably Epictetus knew nothing, is very different. It promises future happiness on certain conditions to Christians, but to Christians only, if I understand it right.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-35" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-36" role="doc-endnote"><p>See the note of Schweig. on this passage.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-36" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-37" role="doc-endnote"><p>The word is <span class="foreign" lang="grc">καρπίστην δίδως</span>. See iii. 24.76 and the note 15: also Upton’s note on this passage. Schweig. says that he does not quite understand why Epictetus here says <span class="foreign" lang="grc">διδόναι καρπίστην</span>, <q>dare vindicem</q> or <q>adsertorem,</q> instead of saying <q>vindicate sese in libertatem.</q></p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-37" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-38" role="doc-endnote"><p>See iii. 24. 66, ii. 13. 24.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-38" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-39" role="doc-endnote"><p>See the same story in Aulus Gellius (<cite>ii. c. 18</cite>), who says that Xeniades, a Corinthian, bought Diogenes, manumitted him and made him the master of his children.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-39" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-40" role="doc-endnote"><p>See Schweig.’s note 15.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-40" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-41" role="doc-endnote"><p>See i. 2, note 5.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-41" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-42" role="doc-endnote"><p>I do not know if dogs sweat; at least in a state of health I have never seen it. But this is a question for the learned in dog science.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-42" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-43" role="doc-endnote"><p>See Schweig.’s note.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-43" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-44" role="doc-endnote"><p>As Upton remarks, Epictetus is referring to the four categories of the Stoics.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-44" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-45" role="doc-endnote"><p>Epictetus, Encheiridion c. 52. M. Antoninus, Gatak. 2d. ed. 1697, Annot. p. 96.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-45" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-46" role="doc-endnote"><p><span class="cit"><span class="verse-quote" lang="lat" class="foreign"><span class="lg"> <span class="l">Stoicus occidit Baream, delator amicum,</span> <span class="l">Discipulumque senex.</span> </span></span> <cite>Juvenal, iii. 116.</cite> </span> Epictetus is supposed to allude to the crime of Egnatius Celer who accused Barea Soranus at Rome in the reign of Nero (<cite>Tacit. Ann. xvi. 32</cite>).</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-46" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-47" role="doc-endnote"><p>Mrs. Carter says that <q>there is much obscurity and some variety of reading in several lines of the original.</q> But see Schweig.’s notes. Epictetus is showing that talk about philosophy is useless: philosophy should be practical.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-47" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-48" role="doc-endnote"><p><cite>Horace Sat. ii. 5</cite>.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-48" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-49" role="doc-endnote"><p>Aprulla is a Roman woman’s name. It means some old woman who is courted for her money.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-49" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-50" role="doc-endnote"><p>Compare Plato (Symposium, p. 206): <q>All men conceive both as to the body and as to the soul, and when they have arrived at a certain age, our nature desires to procreate. But it cannot procreate in that which is ugly, but in that which is beautiful. For the conjunction of man and woman is generation; but this act is divine, and this in the animal which is mortal is divine, conceiving and begetting.</q> See what is said in ii. 23, note 10 on marrying. In a certain sense the procreation of children is a duty, and consequently the providing for them is also a duty. It is the fulfilling of the will and purpose of the Deity to people the earth; and therefore the act of procreation is divine. So a man’s duty is to labour in some way, and if necessary, to earn his living and sustain the life which he has received; and this is also a divine act. Paul’s opinion of marriage is contained in Cor. i. 7. Some of his teaching on this matter has been justly condemned. He has no conception of the true nature of marriage; at least he does not show that he has in this chapter. His teaching is impracticable, contrary to that of Epictetus, and to the nature and constitution of man; and it is rejected by the good sense of Christians who affect to receive his teaching; except, I suppose, by the superstitious body of Christians, who recommend and commend the so-called religious, and unmarried life.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-50" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-51" role="doc-endnote"><p>Felicion. See i. 19, p. 62.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-51" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-52" role="doc-endnote"><p>Epictetus alludes to his lameness: compare i. 8. 14, i. 16. 20, and other passages. Upton.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-52" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-53" role="doc-endnote"><p>Schweig. doubts if the words <span class="foreign" lang="grc">οὐ γὰρ ἡν</span>, which I have omitted, are genuine, and give his reasons for the doubt.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-53" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-54" role="doc-endnote"><p>Schweig. has a note on this difficult passage, which is rather obscure.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-54" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-55" role="doc-endnote"><p>The sense of <q>law</q> (<span class="foreign" lang="grc">ὁ νόμος</span>) can be collected from what follows. Compare the discourse of Socrates on obedience to the law. (Criton, c. 11, etc.)</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-55" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-56" role="doc-endnote"><p>See Schweig.’s note on <span class="foreign" lang="grc">ἀπεριστάτου</span>.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-56" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-57" role="doc-endnote"><p>Socrates fought at Potidaea, Amphipolis and Delium. He is said to have gained the prize for courage at Delium. He was a brave soldier as well as a philosopher, a union of qualities not common. (Plato’s Apology.)</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-57" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-58" role="doc-endnote"><p>Socrates with others was ordered by the Thirty tyrants, who at that time governed Athens, to arrest Leon in the island of Salamis and to bring him to be put to death. But Socrates refused to obey the order. Few men would have done what he did under the circumstances. (Plato’s Apology; M. Antoninus, vii. 66.)</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-58" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-59" role="doc-endnote"><p>Cicero, Tuscul. Disp. i. 29.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-59" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-60" role="doc-endnote"><p>The Dialogue of Plato, named Criton, contains the arguments which were used by his friends to persuade Socrates to escape from prison, and the reply of Socrates.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-60" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-61" role="doc-endnote"><p>This alludes to the behaviour of Socrates when he refused to put to the vote the matter of the Athenian generals and this behaviour after the naval battle of Arginusae. The violence of the weather prevented the commanders from collecting and honorably burying those who fell in the battle; and the Athenians after their hasty fashion, wished all the commanders to be put to death. But Socrates, who was in office at this time, resisted the unjust clamour of the people. Xenophon <cite>Hellenica, i. c. 7, 15</cite>; Plato, Apologia; Xenophon, <cite>Memorab. i. 1, 18</cite></p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-61" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-62" role="doc-endnote"><p>The original is <span class="foreign" lang="grc">ποῦ γὰρ ἂν ἔτι ἔμενον ἐκεῖνοι</span>; this seems to mean, if we had escaped and left the country, where would those have been to whom we might have been useful? They would have been left behind, and we could have done nothing for them.</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-62" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
<li class="note" id="note-63" role="doc-endnote"><p>This is the conclusion about Socrates, whom Epictetus highly valued: the remembrance of what Socrates did and said is even more useful than his life. <q>The life of the dead,</q> says Cicero of Servius Sulpicius, the great Roman jurist and Cicero’s friend, <q>rests in the remembrance of the living.</q> Epictetus has told us of some of the acts of Socrates, which prove him to have been a brave and honest man. He does not tell us here what Socrates said, which means what he taught; but he knew what it was. Modern writers have expounded the matter at length, and in a form which Epictetus would not or could not have used.—Socrates left to others the questions which relate to the material world, and he first taught, as we are told, the things which concern man’s daily life and his intercourse with other men: in other words he taught Ethic (the principles of morality). Fields and trees, he said, will teach me nothing, but man in his social state will; and man then is the proper subject of the philosophy of Socrates. The beginning of this knowledge was as he said, to know himself according to the precept of the Delphic oracle, Know thyself (<span class="foreign" lang="grc">γνῶθι σεαυτόν</span>): and the object of his philosophy was to comprehend the nature of man as a moral being in all relations; and among these the relation of man to God as the father of all, creator and ruler of all, as Plato expresses it. Socrates taught that what we call death is not the end of man; death is only the road to another life. The death of Socrates was conformable to his life and teaching. <q>Socrates died not only with the noblest courage and tranquillity, but he also refused, as we are told, to escape from death, which the laws of the state permitted, by going into exile or paying a fine, because as he said, if he had himself consented to a fine or allowed others to propose it, (Xenophon, <cite>Apol. § 22</cite>), such an act would have been an admission of his guilt. Both (Socrates and Jesus) offered themselves with the firmest resolution for a holy cause, which was so far from being lost through their death that it only served rather to make it the general cause of mankind.</q> (Das Christliche des Platonismus oder Socrates und Christus, by F. C. Baur.)</p> 
<p>This essay by Baur is very ingenious. Perhaps there are some readers who will disagree with him on many points in the comparison of Socrates and Christus. However the essay is well worth the trouble of reading.</p> 
<p>The opinion of Rousseau in his comparison of Jesus and Socrates is in some respects more just than that of Baur, though the learning of the Frenchman is very small when compared with that of the German. <q>What prejudices, what blindness must a man have,</q> says Rousseau, <q>when he dares to compare the son of Sophroniscus with the son of Mary!—The death of Socrates philosophising tranquilly with his friends is the most gentle that a man could desire; that of Jesus expiring in torments, insulted, jeered, cursed by a whole people, is the most horrible that: man could dread. Socrates taking the poisoned cup blesses him who presents it and weeps; Jesus in his horrible punishment prays for his savage executioners. Yes, if the life and the death of Socrates are those of a sage, the life and the death of Jesus are those of a God.</q> (Rousseau, Emile, vol. iii. p. 166. Amsterdam, 1765.)</p><a class="note-back" href="#noteref-63" aria-label="back to the text">&#8617;</a></li>
</ol>
</section>
